**LONG LIVE THE KING: Why Jesus Died and What It Means For Us All  

**The Price of Freedom (Ransom)  
  
**Main Scripture: Mark 10:32-45 NIV  
  
**_Jesus took the Twelve aside and told them what was going to happen to him. “We are going up to Jerusalem,” he said, “and the Son of Man will be delivered over to the chief priests and the teachers of the law. They will condemn him to death and will hand him over to the Gentiles,  who will mock him and spit on him, flog him and kill him. Three days later he will rise.” Then James and John, the sons of Zebedee, came to him. “Teacher,” they said, “we want you to do for us whatever we ask.”  “What do you want me to do for you?” he asked. They replied, “Let one of us sit at your_ **_right_** _and the other at your_ **_left_** _in your glory.”  
“You don’t know what you are asking,” Jesus said. “Can you drink the cup I drink or be baptized with the baptism I am baptized with?” “We can,” they answered. Jesus said to them, “You will drink the cup I drink and be baptized with the baptism I am baptized with,  but to sit at my right or left is not for me to grant. These places belong to those for whom they have been prepared.” When the ten heard about this, they became indignant with James and John. Jesus called them together and said, “You know that those who are regarded as rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their high officials exercise authority over them.  Not so with you. Instead, whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant,  and whoever wants to be first must be slave of all. For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a_ **_ransom_** _for many.”_  
**Additional Scripture:** 

- 1 Corinthians 6:19-20
- 1 Timothy 2:5-6
- Psalm 49:5-8

**Quotes:**

_“The value of any commodity… is equal to the quantity of labor… Labor is alone the ultimate and real standard by which the value of all commodities can at all times and places be estimated and compared. It is their real price.”_  
- **Adam Smith**

_“Christ gave Himself as a ransom for many, buying us from the hands of the devil by His own blood.”_  
- **Origen**

_“God has not stood back and pulled levers. He has stepped into the situation himself, personally. That is in large part what the trope ransom means in the biblical literature. The principal idea is that of_ **_cost to God_**_.”_  
- **Fleming Rutledge**

#### Outline

# “Long Live the King – Ransom”
Sermon by Jay, Westgate Church
Text: [Mark 10:32–45](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark+10%3A32-45&version=ESV)

---

## I. Jay Introduces Himself and the Series Context

1. Greeting and personal introduction
   - “Good morning. Great to see you. If we’ve not met, I’m **Jay**, and I’m so grateful you’re here.”
   - Greets Saratoga room specifically; greets South Hills and Redwood City congregations and expresses joy in the shared journey as one church family.

2. Immediate move into teaching posture
   - States he wants to “jump right in” with a non‑rhetorical question and an image (a painting) to get everyone thinking.

---

## II. Opening Question: What Is Something Worth?

1. Showing the first painting (Cézanne)
   - Displays a painting and asks people, very honestly, “How much would you pay for this?” encouraging blurting out answers (no hand‑raising, don’t overthink).
   - Hears answers like “a dollar,” “five dollars,” “twenty,” “a hundred,” and someone says “a million.”

2. Revelation of the painting’s actual value
   - Identifies the work as a painting by 19th‑century artist **Paul Cézanne**.
   - Says it sold at a Christie’s auction in November 2022 for **$137 million**, noting everyone would have “lost the bid.”

3. Additional paintings from the same auction
   - **“Birch Forest” by Gustav Klimt** – sold for **$104 million** that same night.
   - A **Van Gogh** painting – sold that night for **$117 million**.
   - In total, **60 paintings** sold in one evening for **$1.5 billion**, the most money ever spent in a single art auction in recorded history.

4. Framing the main question
   - Asks rhetorically: *What compels people to spend this kind of money on art?*
   - Notes the discrepancy between initial audience estimates and the actual prices to expose how we think about value.

---

## III. How Do We Determine Value?

1. Modern view: value as price someone will pay
   - Suggests that in the modern world, **worth is often defined by the monetary price** someone is willing to pay.
   - If someone pays $137M for the Cézanne, then “objectively” you can argue it’s worth $137M because that was the price actually paid.

2. Adam Smith and labor as value
   - Introduces **Adam Smith**, 18th‑century philosopher, “father of modern economics.”
   - Summarizes Smith’s idea: the value of a commodity is tied to the **quantity of labor** required to produce it; labor is the “real price.”

3. Illustration: Hilda’s family cookbook
   - Tells a story about an elderly couple, **Chuck and Hilda**, from a previous church.
   - At lunch in their home, Hilda pulls out a **thick, dusty, tattered family cookbook**, passed down over generations.
   - Pages show age at the front and become “newer” as later generations add recipes.
   - To an outsider, you wouldn’t pay much—maybe nothing—for the book, but to Hilda it is a **priceless family heirloom** she longs to pass on.
   - Point: its value is not the market price but the **labor and love** poured into it.

4. Illustration: friends’ newborn baby
   - Mentions several friends in the Westgate family who recently had babies, including a couple in his life group.
   - The journey to parenthood was long and hard; the baby massively disrupts their busy lives and costs them money.
   - The husband sends pictures of his exhausted face on the group text.
   - Yet he “cannot imagine life any other way” – the child is **priceless** despite the cost.
   - Point: true value is defined by the **love and sacrifice** invested, not monetary gain.

---

## IV. Transition to Lent and the Cross: What Are We Worth to God?

1. Series frame: Long Live the King
   - States that in this Lenten season, the church is in a series **“Long Live the King: Why Jesus died and what it means for us all.”**
   - Notes they are exploring **multiple biblical images** that answer *why* Jesus died and *what it means* for us as they journey toward Good Friday and Easter.

2. Focus image for this sermon: ransom
   - Today’s focus is an image that highlights the **immense cost and deep love** expressed on the cross: the image of **ransom**.

3. Scripture: purchased at a price – [1 Corinthians 6:19–20](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1+Corinthians+6%3A19-20&version=ESV)
   - Quotes Paul: “You are not your own; you were bought at a price.”
   - Raises the question: If we were bought at a price, **what was that price**—a dollar, $5, $20, $100, $1M, $137M, or something else?

4. Scripture: Christ as ransom – [1 Timothy 2:5–6](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=1+Timothy+2%3A5-6&version=ESV)
   - Cites: “There is one God and one mediator between God and mankind, the man Christ Jesus, who gave Himself as a ransom for all people.”
   - Emphasizes that **Jesus Himself**—specifically **His life given as ransom**—is the price paid so that we might have life.

5. Our value before God
   - Whatever others say or we believe about ourselves, God determines our worth by **the life of His Son** offered for us.
   - To God, “you were worth His life.”

---

## V. What Does “Ransom” Mean? Early Misunderstandings

1. Historical debate on ransom
   - Notes that the word **“ransom”** has been debated for centuries among Christian theologians.
   - In the early centuries of the church, many thought ransom meant **God paying a price to Satan**.

2. Origen’s view
   - Quotes early church father **Origen**, who said Christ “gave himself as a ransom for many, buying us from the hands of the devil by his own blood.”
   - Explains Origen held some **heretical views**, e.g., he did **not** believe in a literal, physical resurrection of Jesus, which undermines his reliability.

3. Rejection of ransom‑to‑Satan theory
   - States there is **no biblical evidence** that Satan has a legitimate ownership claim on human beings.
   - God does **not** pay Satan off; ransom is not a financial settlement with the devil.
   - This raises the key interpretive question: *If the ransom is not paid to Satan, then what does the ransom imagery really mean?*

---

## VI. Exegesis of Mark 10:32–45 – The Ransom Saying in Context

### A. Jesus Predicts His Passion – [Mark 10:32–34](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark+10%3A32-34&version=ESV)

1. Third passion prediction
   - Jesus takes the Twelve aside and tells them what will happen in Jerusalem: He will be handed over, condemned to death, delivered to the Gentiles, mocked, spat on, flogged, killed, and after three days, He will rise. [Mark 10:32–34](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark+10%3A32-34&version=ESV)

2. The disciples’ self‑interested reaction
   - Immediately after Jesus speaks about suffering and death, **James and John** approach Him with a request.

### B. The Ambitious Request – [Mark 10:35–37](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark+10%3A35-37&version=ESV)

1. “Do for us whatever we ask”
   - James and John say, “Teacher, we want you to do for us **whatever we ask**,” which Jay calls a “ridiculous thing to say” to Jesus, yet notes how often we approach God similarly.

2. Desire for status and glory
   - Their request: “Let one of us sit at your right and the other at your left in your glory.” [Mark 10:37](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark+10%3A37&version=ESV)
   - Jay explains ancient royal thrones: seats at the **right and left** of a king signified **highest honor** in the kingdom.

3. Contrast between Jesus’ mission and their expectations
   - While Jesus talks about **suffering and a cross**, the disciples are dreaming about **status and a throne**.
   - They assume Jesus came primarily to **take power**, but Jesus understands His mission as **laying down power** to make a crucial payment.

### C. “Cup” and “Baptism” – [Mark 10:38–40](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark+10%3A38-40&version=ESV)

1. Jesus’ response
   - “You don’t know what you are asking. Can you drink the cup I drink or be baptized with the baptism I am baptized with?” [Mark 10:38](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark+10%3A38&version=ESV)
   - James and John confidently say, “We can.”

2. Future suffering of the disciples
   - Jesus replies they indeed **will** drink His cup and share His baptism, pointing to their future suffering and martyrdom for the faith after His resurrection.
   - He clarifies that seats at His right and left are not His to grant; they belong to those for whom they have been prepared. [Mark 10:39–40](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark+10%3A39-40&version=ESV)

3. The other disciples’ indignation
   - The remaining ten become **indignant** with James and John. [Mark 10:41](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark+10%3A41&version=ESV)
   - Jay infers their anger is not moral outrage but **jealousy**—they also want those seats and are upset that James and John asked first.

### D. Redefining Greatness and Power – [Mark 10:42–44](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark+10%3A42-44&version=ESV)

1. The Gentile model of leadership
   - Jesus gathers them and contrasts Gentile rulers who “lord it over” people and exercise top‑down authority. [Mark 10:42](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark+10%3A42&version=ESV)

2. The kingdom model
   - “Not so with you.” Greatness in Jesus’ kingdom means becoming a **servant**, and being first means being **slave of all**. [Mark 10:43–44](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark+10%3A43-44&version=ESV)
   - Jesus redefines power as **self‑giving servanthood**, not grasping for status.

### E. The Ransom Statement – [Mark 10:45](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark+10%3A45&version=ESV)

1. Jesus’ mission summarized
   - “For even the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a **ransom for many**.” [Mark 10:45](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Mark+10%3A45&version=ESV)

2. Meaning of “lutron” (ransom)
   - Notes the Greek word **lutron** always carries the idea of **payment** in the ancient world.
   - Three primary uses:
     - Payment to **release slaves or captives**.
     - Payment to **rescue** someone from execution.
     - Payment to **absolve guilt** of an offender.
   - So ransom implies **payment for release or rescue**.

3. What Jesus is saying about His death
   - When Jesus says He came to give His life as a ransom, He means He is **paying the price** for people’s **release and rescue**.
   - His death is a sacrificial payment so that we can be **freed and forgiven**, not a transaction with Satan.

---

## VII. Old Testament Background: No One Can Pay for Life – [Psalm 49:5–9](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Psalm+49%3A5-9&version=ESV)

1. Reading from Psalm 49
   - Quotes the psalmist: those who trust in wealth cannot redeem the life of another or give God a ransom; “the ransom for a life is costly, no payment is ever enough.” [Psalm 49:5–9](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=Psalm+49%3A5-9&version=ESV)

2. Meaning within Psalm 49’s context
   - The psalm’s point: **no amount of wealth can save anyone from death.**
   - You can pay off **debt**, but you cannot pay off **death**.

3. Illustration: Elon Musk and mortality
   - Uses **Elon Musk** as an example: richest person in history, yet he will still die like everyone else.
   - Confirms that human money cannot purchase escape from death.

4. The question that remains
   - If “no one can redeem the life of another” and “no payment is ever enough,” **who can pay the price**?

---

## VIII. The Cross as God’s Costly Payment and Love

1. Jesus pays the price we cannot
   - Returns to Mark 10:45: Jesus gives His life as **ransom**, paying the price that we could never pay.
   - The price is not an amount of money but **His own life and blood**, given to defeat death and bring us life.

2. Fleming Rutledge’s insight
   - Quotes theologian **Fleming Rutledge**: God doesn’t stand far off pulling levers; He **steps into the situation personally**.
   - Ransom points to the **cost to God**—His own self‑giving love.

3. Payment not to Satan, but for our freedom
   - Clarifies again: Jesus’ “payment” is not a payoff to the devil.
   - The cross is God **bearing the immense cost** to **free and unshackle** us from what enslaves us: fear, pain, shame, bondage, guilt, and the consequences of sin.

4. The deadly seriousness of sin
   - The cross shows that **sin is deadly** and leads to death, which was never God’s original intent for humanity.
   - God is willing to **pay the price of that death** Himself so that we can have life.

5. Our worth before God
   - Our value is measured not in millions of dollars, but in the **life of God’s Son**, broken body and shed blood.
   - Jesus, a real person, died believing He was dying so that **you might live**.
   - Therefore, you are not an afterthought, not disposable, not too far gone, and not forgotten.

---

## IX. Living as Those Who Are Ransomed and Free

1. The declaration of freedom
   - Repeats: “If you say yes to Jesus, **you are free**. The price has already been paid.”
   - Asks where we still live as though enslaved—hidden shame, secret struggles, addictions, or idolatrous goals that define our worth.

2. Identity secured
   - Asserts that who you are is already defined; your value and worth are already determined at the cross.
   - It was **love** that took Jesus to the cross, and He did it to **set you free**.

3. Call to respond in worship
   - Invites Chris and the worship team (and teams at other campuses) to come and lead in singing about God’s immense love.
   - Sends South Hills and Redwood City back to their pastors for a final movement of the teaching and response.

---

## X. Auction Metaphor: Competing Bids for Your Soul

1. Returning to the art auction imagery
   - Re‑visits the **Christie’s auction** scene: a room with paddles raised as bids climb—10M, 50M, 100M, etc.
   - Describes how paddles go up and down until one remains at the final, highest price.

2. You as a work of art
   - Invites listeners to imagine themselves as a **work of art** being auctioned.
   - Many things are “bidding” for your soul:
     - The devil, as the enemy of God.
     - Your worries and fears.
     - Your anxieties, failures, flaws, insecurities.
     - Your circumstances, situations, unanswered prayers, unmet expectations, and unfulfilled ambitions.
   - Each of these bids to define you and enslave your soul.

3. The hand that outbids them all
   - Says the cross reveals **one hand** raised that will **outbid them all**.
   - It is the **nail‑pierced, scarred hand of Jesus**, not holding a paddle but bearing a wound of infinite worth.
   - As every other “bidder” tries to claim you, Jesus’ wounded hand stays raised saying, “No, you’re mine.”
   - He offers His **life for your life**, paying a price beyond compare.

4. You as priceless art
   - Affirms that you are a **work of art beyond compare**, loved in **unfathomable ways**.
   - Your worth is the **highest price and greatest cost**: the life of God’s Son, so that you might be called a **child of God**.

5. Scriptural echo: freedom in Christ – [John 8:36](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=John+8%3A36&version=ESV)
   - Cites: “Whoever the Son sets free is free indeed,” applying it to Jesus’ ransom work. [John 8:36](https://www.biblegateway.com/passage/?search=John+8%3A36&version=ESV)

---

## XI. Closing Worship and Invitation

1. Song response: “Jesus Paid It All”
   - Leads the congregation into singing **“Jesus Paid It All”**, repeating lines like:
     - “Jesus paid it all, all to Him I owe.”
     - “Sin had left a crimson stain, He washed it white as snow.”
   - Uses the song to reinforce that Jesus has **fully paid the debt of sin**.

2. Final exhortation about the debt paid
   - Reiterates that Jesus paid **not just any debt**, but the **ultimate debt owed to death** so that we might live now and forever.

3. Prayer invitation
   - Invites the **prayer team** forward.
   - Extends a specific invitation to those exploring faith who realize they’ve never truly considered that **death need not be the end** of their story because of Jesus’ death and resurrection.
   - Also invites anyone carrying heavy burdens to come receive prayer.

4. Sending and benediction
   - Sends the congregation out to live in the **confidence, courage, and comfort** of knowing they are **free** and the debt of sin has been fully paid.
   - Encourages them to go in **grace, peace, and love**, reminding them again that the price is paid by Christ our Savior.
